objectives.title: Audit cryptographic dependency usage
objectives.summary: Workspace and crate cryptographic dependencies, feature selection, algorithm dispatch, and safe API usage were reviewed. The audited paths use a narrow dependency set, safe high-level AEAD APIs, and fail-closed dispatch for unsupported non-AEAD modes.

objectives.title: Audit authentication failure behavior
objectives.summary: Archive and transport authentication failures were traced through success and failure paths. The audited implementations fail closed, reject post-binding plaintext in TLS_EXPORTER sessions, and avoid releasing plaintext before authentication succeeds.

objectives.title: Audit TLS_EXPORTER SAR-AEAD key derivation
objectives.summary: TLS_EXPORTER KMS parsing, context encoding, transport exporter integration, and negative-path evidence were reviewed. Unsupported AEAD and Global Header hash IDs and mismatched derived-key lengths are accepted by parsing and remain unvalidated by in-repo consumers, so unsupported or inconsistent TLS_EXPORTER parameters are not guaranteed to fail closed end-to-end.

objectives.title: Audit AAD binding behavior
objectives.summary: AAD construction across archive, selective-FEC, and additional QUIC control-stream paths was reviewed. Current selective-FEC and transport controls were verified, and the previously recorded unchecked Global Flags length narrowing in AAD construction remains relevant to this objective.

objectives.title: Audit AEAD tag failure behavior
objectives.summary: AEAD tag parsing and failure behavior were reviewed across archive and transport call paths. Tag failures are treated as hard errors for the authenticated unit and do not permit continued processing of unauthenticated plaintext.

objectives.title: Audit constant-time handling of secret comparisons where comparison is unavoidable
objectives.summary: Secret-dependent comparisons in the audited scope were reviewed. Digest equality uses a constant-time helper, and AEAD tag verification remains inside vetted crypto library operations rather than open-coded byte comparisons.

objectives.title: Audit zeroization of exporter-derived material where practical
objectives.summary: Zeroization practicality was reviewed for CEKs, derived keys, password material, and failure buffers. The audited crypto paths consistently wrap secret material in zeroizing containers and explicitly clear plaintext buffers on authentication failure.

objectives.title: Audit logs, errors, debug APIs, and test helpers for accidental secret exposure
objectives.summary: Errors, debug exposure surfaces, CLI secret-entry paths, precedence, and user-facing guidance were reviewed. A safer interactive password path already exists, but current CLI help and documentation do not clearly warn against argv/environment exposure channels or consistently prefer the safer path.

objectives.title: Audit decompressor setup limits and decoded output bounds
objectives.summary: Decompressor decoded output is bounded by max_output_size via copy_bounded before any decompressed byte reaches the caller; algorithm IDs are validated before decoder construction; and the STORE, DEFLATE, and ZSTD paths all route through the same bounded copy path. SAR documentation does not currently state that decoder library-internal working memory is outside the documented ResourceLimits surface; that documentation gap is recorded in M13-TRANSFORM-008.

objectives.title: Audit patch and delta setup limits
objectives.summary: BSDIFF and VCDIFF limits (patch size, block counts, output size) are correctly derived from unified ResourceLimits via adapter functions before patch application. However, the complete fuzz target inventory does not meaningfully reach BSDIFF or VCDIFF patch application with attacker-controlled base-plus-patch inputs, and no fuzz target reaches the archive-level repair APIs; that narrowed gap is recorded in M13-TRANSFORM-007.

objectives.title: Audit algorithm-switching and profile-based algorithm restrictions
objectives.summary: SAR archives use per-entry algorithm IDs read from each LFH; unsupported or reserved IDs fail closed at decode time with no per-session algorithm-switching state to exploit. However, the specification does not define per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables, leaving implementors without a basis to enforce profile-specific algorithm constraints before entry processing. No unsafe code was found in any audited transform or recovery crate.

objectives.title: Audit delta target-size and output-size invariants
objectives.summary: Declared target size (LFH Uncompressed Size) is verified after patch application for all implemented algorithms. STORE_PATCH, BSDIFF, and VCDIFF all return PatchFailed when reconstructed output length does not equal the declared size. Arithmetic throughout the BSDIFF and VCDIFF implementations uses checked operations.

objectives.title: Audit sparse reconstruction limits
objectives.summary: Sparse reconstruction allocates exactly logical_size bytes, bounded before allocation by max_decoded_entry_size and max_allocation_bytes. Extent validation uses checked arithmetic, enforces non-overlapping ascending-offset order, and rejects zero-length extents, out-of-bounds extents, and excess payload bytes. Fragment group validation enforces count, group span, and loss-tolerant gap limits before reassembly.

objectives.title: Audit FEC and recovery metadata bounds
objectives.summary: FEC value byte length is bounded by check_fec_value_bytes before codec construction in both LFH and recovery TLV paths. XOR and RS codecs independently enforce a 256 MiB MAX_PARITY_SIZE constant on parity allocation. Stripe, group, and parity products use checked arithmetic throughout. Recovery TLV IDs outside the defined range are rejected before value parsing.

objectives.title: Audit in-memory recovery API limitations
objectives.summary: The `repair_archive` API is explicitly documented as an in-memory API and applies `max_archive_size`, `max_recovery_protected_range`, and a partial `max_repair_working_set` check before repair execution. Tracing source-visible ownership at `Vec::with_capacity(archive_bytes.len())` (during repaired-output allocation in `repair_archive()`): `layout.recovery_tlvs` (`R` bytes) and `erasure_indices` (`E` bytes) remain in scope and allocated alongside the caller-owned archive slice (`X`), the recovered protected-range output (`P`), and the repaired full-archive output being allocated (`X`). The minimum proven repaired-output peak is `2X + P`; the full source-visible peak is at least `2X + P + R + E`. The checked formula `X + 2P + T` does not match the source-visible repaired-output lifetime set: it omits the repaired output `X`, omits most of `R` and all of `E`, and includes a second `protected_range.length` term that has no corresponding source-visible live allocation at that peak; the total simultaneous retained memory is therefore undercounted.

objectives.title: Audit profile-specific strict-mode rejection behavior
objectives.summary: validate_archive_profile checks global-flag constraints per profile. Per-entry algorithm ID validation is documented as a known limitation not yet implemented. The specification requires returning SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED for algorithm IDs not supported by the selected profile but does not provide per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables; this specification gap is recorded.

objectives.title: Audit archive path validation and normalization behavior
objectives.summary: Archive entry names and symlink parent components are lexically validated before joining to the output tree; absolute, UNC, drive-prefixed, empty, dot, and dot-dot components are rejected, and existing symlink parents are refused.

objectives.title: Audit output-root confinement and replacement-race behavior
objectives.summary: The extractor performs lexical checks but does not canonicalize or hold directory-relative handles for final create, rename, or metadata operations, so output-root symlinks and concurrent path replacement remain security-relevant.

objectives.title: Audit symlink target semantics and hardlink handling
objectives.summary: Hardlink creation is absent from the current entry model and extractor, and symlink extraction stays opt-in, but the specification does not yet resolve whether escaping or absolute symlink targets are conforming archive content or must be rejected for extraction safety.

objectives.title: Audit permission restoration and directory staging/finalization ordering
objectives.summary: New directories are staged with a chmod to mode 0o700 that succeeds before any archive content is written (failing closed on error); directory metadata is finalized after child extraction in reverse-depth order; and restored permission modes are masked to ordinary permission bits. The initial creation via `fs::create_dir()` uses the process umask, so the directory exists briefly at a umask-determined mode before the chmod; during that window the directory is empty and other local principals with parent-directory access can observe its existence but cannot write to it under ordinary mode-bit semantics.

objectives.title: Audit owner and timestamp restoration hazards
objectives.summary: Owner and timestamp restoration are opt-in and symlink metadata application is skipped, but the underlying path-based metadata calls inherit the unresolved confinement and race issue tracked separately.

objectives.title: Audit platform-specific extraction safety branches
objectives.summary: Non-Unix builds fail closed when symlink extraction or owner or permission restoration is requested, so the Unix-only mutation paths remain the platform-specific extraction surface reviewed here.

objectives.title: Crate-boundary attack surface
objectives.summary: The primary crate-boundary risk identified is that `TransportConfig` propagates only `max_active_streams` into the `ResourceLimits` used by `StreamArchiveParser` and `SessionManager` inside `InMemoryTransport`, leaving all other limits at their defaults. This fixed-default boundary contract is undocumented at the transport API boundary. The reviewed crate roots for `sar-transport`, `sar-stream`, `sar-archive`, `sar-compression`, `sar-delta`, `sar-fec`, `sar-fragmentation`, `sar-loss-tolerant`, `sar-sparse`, `sar-crypto`, and `sar-core` all carry `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. No reviewed cross-crate ownership, aliasing, or lifetime assumption risks were found beyond the documented `KeyProvider` trait-object callback model addressed in FFI objectives.

objectives.title: Profile and library-layout attack surface
objectives.summary: `validate_archive_profile` is explicitly documented as global-header-only and does not enforce entry-level algorithm restrictions, per-entry LOSS_TOLERANT presence, or unsafe path rejection. The reviewed public `sar-archive` profile API surface is limited to `ComplianceProfile`, `ProfileReport`, `validate_archive_profile`, and profile name conversion helpers; no reviewed public entry-iterating profile-validation entry point was identified. The `Standard` profile variant is a placeholder. The normative algorithm restriction tables that would back per-entry algorithm enforcement remain unresolved and are tracked in M13-TRANSFORM-001. Profile state is not carried through the transport or session layer; callers must apply profile validation separately. No additional profile-bypass paths or unsafe component compositions were identified in the reviewed profile, transport, and session artifacts.

objectives.title: Transport and session attack surface
objectives.summary: The transport inactivity watchdog is caller-opt-in and the activation requirement is not documented at the `TransportConfig` level. `QuicSarConnection::feed_stream_bytes` requires a follow-up `flush_pending_control_frames` call to emit outbound control frames, but this ordering requirement is absent from the public method docstring. Both are documentation gaps. A positive control was confirmed: `InMemoryTransport` enforces fail-closed behavior for TLS_EXPORTER-bound sessions at the transport parsing layer, rejecting unencrypted entries before any downstream processing. TLS_EXPORTER KMS parameter validation and AEAD fail-closed behavior are tracked in M13-CRYPTO-001 and M13-CRYPTO-004 respectively and are not duplicated here.

objectives.title: FFI-readiness risks
objectives.summary: Three FFI-readiness gaps were identified: (1) the `KeyProvider` trait callback model requires a purpose-built stable wrapper for any foreign binding because it uses Rust-specific trait objects, `Send + Sync` bounds, and zeroizing secret containers; (2) `SarError::Io(std::io::Error)` is not ABI-stable and must be mapped to `SarStatus` codes before crossing a language boundary; (3) the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs are `async fn` and require a Tokio runtime adapter for synchronous C or Python wrappers, while the TCP binding is synchronous and more amenable to blocking wrappers. None of these is a security finding; all are documentation gaps requiring remediation in M13b.4.

objectives.title: Public Rust APIs exposing unstable layout, ownership, or lifetime assumptions
objectives.summary: Across the reviewed source artifacts and public API inventory entries, no reviewed API was found to rely on stable foreign-compatible memory layout, stable Rust discriminants, unsafe aliasing, or unsound lifetime assumptions. The reviewed public surfaces include ordinary safe Rust ownership forms, borrowed references, `&'static str`, trait objects, and generic I/O, but those forms are not presented as stable FFI representations. No `repr(C)`, `transmute`, `from_raw`, `into_raw`, `offset_of`, `size_of`, or `align_of` usage was found in the reviewed source artifacts. The absence of layout-stability claims is consistent with the API inventory's `readiness: candidate` status for most types.

objectives.title: APIs that should remain Rust-only
objectives.summary: `SecretBytes` and `SecretString` (sar-crypto) should remain Rust-only because they are zeroizing containers whose ownership and destruction semantics cannot be safely transferred across a foreign boundary. `BinaryWriter` and `ParseCursor` (sar-core) are internal parsing and writing helpers not intended as stable surface; they are marked `candidate: false` in the API inventory. `StreamArchiveParser`, `StreamWriteState`, `StreamStep`, `StreamEvent`, and `StreamArchiveSummary` (sar-archive) are marked `not_ready` in the inventory and depend on `Box<dyn KeyProvider>` and generic I/O that require purpose-built wrappers before any foreign exposure. No additional Rust-only classification beyond the API inventory's existing recommendations was required.

objectives.title: APIs potentially suitable for future C or Python wrappers
objectives.summary: Plausible wrapper candidates with ordinary conversion include: `SarStatus` (ready integer enum), `GlobalFlags` (uint32 bitmask), simple metadata structs (`EntryKind`, `EntryPermissionMetadata`, `EntryTimestampMetadata`, `EntryCompressionMetadata`), `ResourceLimits` (flat config struct), `CompressionAlgorithm`, and `validate_archive_profile` paired with `ComplianceProfile`. Candidates requiring a purpose-built stable wrapper include: `ArchiveReader`/`ArchiveWriter` (generic I/O; need opaque handles and owned-buffer operations), `SessionManager` (complex state machine; suitable only through explicit create/step/destroy lifecycle), `KeyProvider` (blocked by M13-FFI-001), and QUIC APIs (blocked by M13-FFI-003). `SarError` requires the `SarStatus` mapping described in M13-FFI-002 before use in any wrapper. APIs that should remain Rust-only for concrete reasons are classified in OBJ-06.

objectives.summary: All M13a.5 actionable findings (M13-BOUNDARY-001, M13-BOUNDARY-002, M13-TRANSPORT-001, M13-TRANSPORT-002, M13-FFI-001, M13-FFI-002, M13-FFI-003) are documentation gaps assigned to M13b.4. findings.title: Unchecked `as u16` narrowing conversion in `global_header_flags_bytes`
findings.summary: `global_header_flags_bytes()` uses an unchecked `as u16` narrowing conversion for the flags size. Under default limits the cast is safe, but with non-default or unlimited limits the cast silently truncates, producing incorrect AEAD AAD bytes.
findings.current_behavior: `global_header_flags_bytes()` casts `header.flags_bytes.len()` (a usize) to u16 using `as u16` without a checked conversion. When `max_global_flags_bytes` is set above u16::MAX or `ResourceLimits::unlimited()` is in effect, the cast silently truncates, producing incorrect AAD bytes for AEAD computation.
findings.expected_behavior: The flags size must be encoded into the AAD bytes using a checked conversion that returns an error on overflow rather than silently truncating.
findings.impact: Silent truncation at AAD construction would cause AEAD authentication to fail for all encrypted entries when the flags buffer exceeds 65535 bytes, without a clear overflow error at the point of failure. Not exploitable under default limits.

evidence.description: `let flags_size = header.flags_bytes.len() as u16;` - unchecked narrowing conversion from usize to u16

evidence.locator: function `write_global_header()`, checked conversion of Global Flags byte length
evidence.description: `write_global_header` uses `u16::try_from(...)` for size encoding at the same location; the inconsistency is clear.

requirements: Use a checked conversion when encoding the Global Flags byte length into the u16 AAD field and return the appropriate existing error on overflow.

notes: Under default ResourceLimits, flags_bytes.len() <= 65535 == u16::MAX, so no truncation occurs in practice. The risk only materializes with non-default or unlimited limits.

acceptance_criteria: Test that `global_header_flags_bytes` returns an error when flags buffer length exceeds u16::MAX under non-default limits.

findings.title: `audit()` data-area scan lacks entry-count limit check
findings.summary: `ArchiveReader::audit()` retains one `ArchiveAuditEntryReport` per scanned entry without enforcing the configured maximum entry count before retaining the report.

evidence.description: No `check_entry_count` call in the `audit()` loop body before `entries.push(...)`.
`limits.check_entry_count(file_count_usize)?;` is present in `parse_central_dictionary()` but not replicated in the data-area scan paths.

notes: `verify()` retains offsets rather than full audit reports, and `next_entry()` does not retain prior reports. This finding is limited to the retained-report behavior of `audit()`.

The minimum parseable LFH estimate in the audit record is 20 bytes with no optional fields, zero payload, and a zero-length name; the estimate is illustrative rather than a practical allocation forecast.

acceptance_criteria: Deterministic test verifying audit() returns LimitExceeded when entry count exceeds the configured limit. Use a small explicit limit (e.g., 2 allowed entries) and a valid archive containing more entries than the limit.

findings.current_behavior: The `audit()` data-area scan advances through parseable entries and pushes one `ArchiveAuditEntryReport` into its retained `entries` vector for each entry. The loop does not call `ResourceLimits::check_entry_count` before the push, so `max_entry_count` does not bound the number of retained reports. `verify()` retains offsets in a separate vector and `next_entry()` does not itself retain prior reports; those paths must not be conflated with the primary `audit()` allocation behavior.
findings.impact: For attacker-controlled archives, retained report memory and scan CPU can grow linearly with the number of parseable entries inside the permitted archive region rather than stopping at `max_entry_count`. The report vector has nontrivial inline storage per entry, and populated owned fields may add per-entry allocations. Archive size still provides an outer bound, but the default archive-size ceiling permits far more entries than the default entry-count limit and can cause memory exhaustion or prolonged processing before the scan ends.

requirements: Maintain a checked running entry count in `audit()` and enforce `max_entry_count` before retaining another `ArchiveAuditEntryReport`.
Return the existing limit-exceeded status without changing unrelated archive parsing or wire-format behavior.
constraints: Use a deterministic regression test with a deliberately small configured limit.

findings.title: TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F accepted in violation of specification
findings.summary: The `classify_type()` function in tlv.rs leaves TLV type IDs 0x05..=0x0F to a wildcard accept arm. The specification explicitly reserves these IDs and requires a reserved-value error. The parser is fail-open for these IDs.
findings.current_behavior: `classify_type()` covers 0x00 (rejected), 0x01-0x04 (accepted), 0x10-0x1F (FEC dispatch), 0x20-0x2F (rejected), 0x30-0x3F (accepted), 0x40/0x41/0x4F (CDC accepted), 0x42-0x4E (rejected), 0x50-0xFF (rejected), and `_` wildcard (accepted). IDs 0x05..=0x0F fall to the wildcard and are parsed, accumulated, and returned without error.
findings.expected_behavior: Reserved TLV type IDs 0x05..=0x0F must be rejected with a reserved-value status before any accumulate or accept path. The dispatch must be exhaustive and fail closed for every possible input byte.
findings.impact: The parser accepts values that the specification designates as reserved and maps to a reserved-value error. This is a confirmed conformance and interoperability defect. No independent security bypass is demonstrated by the audit evidence, so severity is low while remediation priority remains high.

evidence.description: Explicit RESERVED designation for TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F. The specification requires reserved values produce SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE.
`classify_type()` wildcard arm accepts 0x05-0x0F without error; gap in explicit range coverage.

normative_basis.requirement: TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F are RESERVED. Reserved values must produce SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE.

requirements: Reject every reserved TLV type ID in 0x05..=0x0F with the specified reserved-value status before any accumulation or acceptance path.
Keep TLV type classification exhaustive and fail closed for every possible input byte.

acceptance_criteria: Test that each TLV type ID in 0x05..=0x0F is rejected with a reserved-value error by `parse_tlvs`.

findings.title: `GlobalFlags` undefined bits and extension bytes - normative behavior undefined
findings.summary: The specification does not explicitly define how SAR v1.0 readers must handle undefined bits in the first 32 Global Flags bits or nonzero extension bytes beyond the first four bytes. Current implementation behavior is recorded, but normative resolution is required before that behavior can be assessed or changed.
findings.current_behavior: Both `parse_global_header()` and `ArchiveReader::read_global_header()` call `GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate()` to parse the 32-bit flags word, silently discarding bits 6, 7, 11-15, 21-23, and 31. Extension bytes beyond the first 4 bytes are stored but not semantically validated. `validate_global_flags()` does not reject unrecognized bits.
findings.normative_question: 1. Must undefined bits in the first 32-bit Global Flags word be zero? 2. Are additional Global Flags bytes an extensibility mechanism? 3. If additional bytes are allowed, how must unknown nonzero bits in those bytes be handled by a SAR v1.0 implementation? 4. Which SAR status applies when unsupported or reserved global-flag bits are encountered?

evidence.description: `GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate(u32::from_le_bytes(low))` silently drops undefined bits.
`GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate(u32::from_le_bytes(low))` - same pattern in reader path.

evidence.locator: function `validate_global_flags()`, undefined-bit and extension-byte validation rules
evidence.description: `validate_global_flags()` checks only specific flag combinations; does not reject unrecognized bits.
No explicit MUST-be-zero requirement for undefined bits in the 32-bit Global Flags word.

findings.title: `parse_lfh` fuzz targets omit several LFH-layout-affecting global flags
findings.summary: The `parse_lfh` and `parse_lfh_wide` fuzz targets use an 8-bit selector that maps to 8 GlobalFlags constants, producing up to 256 combinations of those 8 selected flags. Six flags that add physical fields to the LFH layout (COMPRESSED, HAS_DELTA, ENCRYPTED, CDC_SUPPORT, PER_FILE_CRC, DEDUPLICATION) are not included in the selector and are never set.
findings.impact: Parser paths for ENCRYPTED, HAS_DELTA, COMPRESSED, CDC_SUPPORT, PER_FILE_CRC, and DEDUPLICATION LFH optional fields are not covered by the dedicated `parse_lfh` or `parse_lfh_wide` targets. Coverage is partially compensated by `archive_entry_decode`, `archive_audit`, and `pr4_lfh_metadata_edges`, but isolated LFH parser coverage for those flag combinations is absent from the dedicated targets.

evidence.description: `lfh_flags()` function covers 8 flags (bits 0-7 of selector) but omits COMPRESSED, HAS_DELTA, ENCRYPTED, CDC_SUPPORT, PER_FILE_CRC, DEDUPLICATION.
Same `lfh_flags()` design as parse_lfh.rs; same omissions.

requirements: Extend the dedicated LFH fuzzing inputs so every Global Flags value that changes the physical LFH layout is independently and combinatorially reachable.
Apply equivalent coverage to both the standard and wide LFH fuzz targets.

notes: `archive_entry_decode` and `archive_audit` partially compensate by exercising full archive parsing including encrypted/compressed entries, but those targets drive higher-level code paths. Isolated LFH parser coverage for these flag combinations is still valuable.
HAS_SYMLINKS does not add any field to the LFH physical layout and is correctly omitted from the layout-affecting list.

findings.title: `archive_structural` fuzz target name overstates coverage scope
findings.summary: The `archive_structural` fuzz target calls only `read_global_header()` and does not exercise entry-walking paths. The target name implies broader structural coverage. findings.title: Extractor does not enforce canonicalized, directory-relative confinement for final filesystem mutations
findings.summary: The CLI extractor lexically validates archive names and checks existing parent components with `symlink_metadata()`, but it never canonicalizes the selected output root or final target before write, rename, chmod, chown, or timestamp operations. Because those final mutations use ordinary path-based filesystem calls, a pre-existing output-root symlink or a concurrent path-replacement race can redirect extraction effects outside the intended root.
findings.current_behavior: `extract_archive()` creates `output_dir` with `create_dir_all()` and then passes the raw path through `prepare_output_file_path()` and `ensure_parent_directory_path()`. Those helpers walk components with `symlink_metadata()` and `create_dir()` checks, but `write_bytes_via_temp()`, `write_sparse_payload_via_temp()`, `finalize_temp_file()`, `extract_symlink_entry()`, `apply_file_metadata()`, and `finalize_directory_metadata()` all perform their final create, rename, remove, chmod, chown, or timestamp operations through ordinary path-based APIs without canonicalizing the resolved target or holding directory-relative handles across the check/use boundary.
findings.expected_behavior: Before each filesystem mutation, extraction should resolve and confine the effective target beneath the selected extraction root using symlink-safe canonicalization and/or directory-relative operations so that later path replacement cannot redirect writes or metadata restoration outside the permitted tree.
findings.impact: An attacker who can influence pre-existing filesystem state for the chosen extraction destination, or who can concurrently replace path components inside an attacker-writable extraction tree, can redirect file creation, atomic rename, symlink creation, or post-write metadata restoration outside the intended root. If extraction is run with `--preserve-owner`, successful exploitation can also redirect privileged ownership changes to an attacker-chosen target path.

evidence.description: `extract_archive()` accepts the caller-supplied `output_dir`, calls `create_dir_all()`, then performs reconstructed-file writes and final directory metadata application through raw `PathBuf` values without canonicalizing the extraction root.

`prepare_output_file_path()` and `ensure_parent_directory_path()` join unchecked `output_dir` prefixes with lexical archive components, inspect parents with `symlink_metadata()`, and create directories with `create_dir()`/`set_permissions()`, but never prove the final resolved path remains beneath a canonical root.

Temporary output paths are derived from the final `Path`, opened with `create_new`, and published with `rename()` using ordinary path resolution; no directory handle or post-resolution confinement check is retained across the check/use window.

File and directory metadata restoration re-checks paths with `symlink_metadata()` but then calls `chown`, `set_file_times`, and `set_permissions` by path, so later replacement can change which inode receives the mutation.

evidence.locator: Section 22.4 `Path Security`, canonicalization and extraction-root confinement requirements
evidence.description: Before any write operation, target paths MUST be canonicalized, all symbolic links and segments MUST be resolved, and extraction MUST ensure the final path resides within the intended extraction root.

Implementations MUST resolve all symbolic links and segments to ensure the final path resides within the intended extraction root. If canonicalization fails or points outside the allowed scope, the implementation MUST return `SAR_ERR_IO` and MUST NOT attempt to create the file.

findings.title: Staging chmod to 0o700 precedes child extraction; directory metadata finalization is deferred and occurs in reverse-depth order
findings.summary: On Unix, `create_restrictive_directory()` calls `fs::create_dir()` (which applies the process umask, typically yielding mode 0o755 with the standard umask of 0o022) and then calls `fs::set_permissions(path, 0o700)` as a separate step. Content extraction for a directory proceeds only after the `set_permissions` call succeeds; if it fails, extraction halts. Pending directory metadata is applied only after child extraction completes and in reverse-depth order, regular-file metadata is applied after temp-file publication, symlink metadata application is skipped, and restored modes are masked to ordinary permission bits so setuid, setgid, and sticky bits are not reintroduced.

evidence.description: `create_restrictive_directory()` calls `fs::create_dir(path)` to create the directory and then calls `fs::set_permissions(path, Permissions::from_mode(0o700))` on Unix. `fs::create_dir` passes mode 0o777 to the `mkdir` syscall, which applies the process umask; with the standard umask of 0o022 the effective creation mode is 0o755. The chmod is a separate step and not atomic with creation. Content extraction proceeds only after `set_permissions` returns `Ok(())`; if it returns an error, extraction halts.

`apply_file_metadata()` runs only after file publication, skips symlink paths, `finalize_directory_metadata()` applies directory metadata after child extraction in reverse depth order, and `apply_permissions()` masks restored modes with `0o0777`.
CLI tests verify directory permissions are applied after extraction and that restoring `0o4755` results in `0o755` on disk.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.4: content extraction for a directory proceeds only after `set_permissions(0o700)` succeeds (failing closed on error), final directory metadata is deferred until children are extracted in reverse-depth order, symlink metadata application is skipped, and special mode bits are stripped from restored permissions. Directory staging uses a create-then-chmod sequence; the initial creation mode is umask-determined (typically 0o755), but the directory is empty and unwritable by other principals during that window, and extraction content is written only after the chmod to 0o700 succeeds.

findings.title: `repair_archive` undercounts total live memory against `max_repair_working_set` at the repaired-output peak
findings.summary: In `repair_archive`, the checked working-set formula is `archive_bytes.len() + 2 * protected_range.length + tlv_value.len()` (`X + 2P + T`). Tracing source-visible ownership at the point where `Vec::with_capacity(archive_bytes.len())` executes (during repaired output allocation in `repair_archive()`): the caller-owned input archive slice (`X` bytes), the SAR-owned cloned RECOVERY TLV storage in `layout.recovery_tlvs` (`R` bytes, still in lexical scope and not dropped), the `erasure_indices` vector (`E` bytes, built before the codec call and still in scope), and the recovered protected-range output (`P` bytes) are all live when the repaired full-archive output (`X` bytes) is allocated. The minimum proven repaired-output peak is therefore at least `2X + P`; including all source-visible retained allocations the peak is at least `2X + P + R + E`. The checked formula `X + 2P + T` omits the repaired output `X`, omits the majority of `R` and all of `E`, and includes a second `protected_range.length` term that does not correspond to any source-visible live allocation at the repaired-output peak; the formula therefore does not match the source-visible repaired-output lifetime set and can pass even when total simultaneous retained memory exceeds `max_repair_working_set`.
findings.current_behavior: Source-visible ownership and drop boundaries in `repair_archive`: (1) `parse_archive_layout` returns an owned `ArchiveLayout` bound to `layout`; `layout.recovery_tlvs` is a `Vec<(u8, Vec<u8>)>` that clones every RECOVERY TLV value from the Central Dictionary (`R` bytes total, bounded indirectly by `max_cd_bytes`, `max_tlv_count`, `max_tlv_bytes`, and `max_fec_value_bytes`); `layout` is not moved or explicitly dropped before the function returns, so the cloned TLV storage remains allocated for the full duration of `repair_archive`. (2) `tlv_value` (the matching TLV's value) is a borrow (`&[u8]`) into `layout.recovery_tlvs`; a borrow ending does not free the backing owned allocation. `protected_bytes` is a borrow into `archive_bytes`; no independent copy is made. `erasure_indices` is an owned `Vec<Erasure>` (`E` bytes) built before the codec call and passed by reference into `recover()`; it is not explicitly dropped after the codec returns and remains in lexical scope at the repaired-output allocation step in `repair_archive()`, so it is live at the repaired-output peak. (3) During FEC recovery, SAR allocates the recovered protected-range output (`P` bytes, bounded by `max_recovery_protected_range`) as the `recovered` `Vec<u8>`; codec-internal temporaries (scratch vectors, matrix buffers, stripe-level allocations) are owned entirely inside the `recover()` call and are freed before it returns. (4) `Vec::with_capacity(archive_bytes.len())` at the repaired-output allocation step in `repair_archive()` allocates the repaired full-archive output (`X` bytes). At that repaired-output allocation step the source-visible live allocations are: caller-owned archive slice backing (`X`), `layout.recovery_tlvs` (`R`), `erasure_indices` (`E`), and `recovered` (`P`). Minimum proven repaired-output peak (unavoidable buffers): `2X + P` (caller input + recovered output + repaired output). Full source-visible repaired-output peak (all owned heap allocations still live in `repair_archive`): at least `2X + P + R + E`. The checked formula at the initial working-set check in `repair_archive()` is `X + 2P + T` (where `T = tlv_value.len()`, a property of the matching TLV already counted within `R`). The formula does not match the source-visible repaired-output lifetime set: it omits the repaired output `X`, omits most of `R` (capturing only the single matching TLV size `T` rather than all cloned TLVs), omits `E`, and includes a second `protected_range.length` term that does not correspond to any source-visible live allocation at the repaired-output peak. A merely unused variable does not establish an audit-visible deallocation guarantee; `layout` and `erasure_indices` are live until they leave scope or are explicitly dropped.
findings.impact:
Because the implementation counts the caller-owned archive input inside the checked formula, the documented/implemented intent of `max_repair_working_set` is to bound total simultaneous retained memory for the in-memory repair operation. The current check can still pass while that total is exceeded. 

Concrete example: `max_archive_size = 100 MiB`, `max_recovery_protected_range = 32 MiB`, protected range `P = 32 MiB`, archive size `X = 100 MiB`, matching RECOVERY TLV size `T = 1 MiB`, `max_repair_working_set = 165 MiB`. Existing checked estimate `X + 2P + T = 100 + 64 + 1 = 165 MiB` - the current check passes. Minimum proven retained memory at the repaired-output peak: `2X + P = 200 + 32 = 232 MiB`, which exceeds the 165 MiB limit. Additional retained layout storage `R` (all cloned RECOVERY TLVs, >= T) and erasure-index storage `E` make the actual source-visible peak higher than 232 MiB; 232 MiB is a lower bound, not the exact total. The reported minimum peak (`2X + P`) is a lower bound because `R` and `E` are not included; an exact formula is impractical without constraining the number and size of all RECOVERY TLVs and the erasure-index count.

findings.title: Per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables are not defined in the specification
findings.summary: The specification requires (Section 12.4 `Unsupported Features`) that implementations return `SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED` for algorithm IDs not supported by the selected profile. However, the specification does not define per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables for compression, delta, FEC, sparse, or recovery algorithms. Without these tables, implementations cannot consistently enforce profile-specific algorithm constraints. `validate_archive_profile` in `crates/sar-archive/src/profile.rs` documents this as a known limitation.
findings.current_behavior: `validate_archive_profile` in `crates/sar-archive/src/profile.rs` validates only global-flag constraints per profile (NO_INDEX, ENCRYPTED). Its documentation explicitly notes: 'Algorithm ID checks are not yet implemented (requires entry iteration).' The specification (Section 12.4 `Unsupported Features`) states that algorithm IDs not supported by the selected profile MUST return SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED, but the specification provides no per-profile algorithm allowlist.
findings.normative_question: Which specific compression, delta, FEC, sparse, and recovery algorithm IDs are allowed or disallowed by each named compliance profile (MinimalInteroperableArchive, StaticArchive, Package, StreamPackage, Backup, Telemetry, LiveMedia, Standard)? At what point in archive processing (archive open, global-header parse, or per-entry decode) must profile-level algorithm validation occur to be considered conformant? How should implementations report profile violations detected during per-entry decode (SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED vs. SAR_ERR_PROFILE_VIOLATION)?

evidence.locator: Section 12.4 `Unsupported Features`, assigned algorithm identifier not implemented by selected profile
evidence.description: Normative requirement: 'If an implementation supports a feature but encounters an assigned algorithm identifier that is not implemented by the selected profile, it MUST return SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED.' No per-profile algorithm table is provided in the specification.

`validate_archive_profile` documentation explicitly notes: 'Algorithm ID checks are not yet implemented (requires entry iteration).' The function validates only NO_INDEX and ENCRYPTED global flags per profile.

findings.title: Decompressor decoded output is bounded by `max_output_size` before any output reaches the caller
findings.summary: All three decompression algorithms (STORE, DEFLATE, ZSTD) route through `copy_bounded`, which checks a running decoded-byte counter using `checked_add` before each 8 192-byte write and returns `LimitExceeded` before writing any chunk that would exceed `max_output_size`. The `decode_payload` function additionally rejects inputs whose `expected_output_size` exceeds `max_output_size` before constructing any decompressor. Algorithm IDs are validated via `CompressionAlgorithm::from_id` before decoder construction, failing closed for reserved and unsupported IDs.

evidence.locator: function `copy_bounded()`, decoded-output cap enforcement before writes
evidence.description: `copy_bounded` maintains a running decoded-byte counter with `u64::try_from` and `checked_add` overflow guards and returns `LimitExceeded` before writing any 8 192-byte chunk that would cause the total to exceed `max_output_size`.

`decode_stream` dispatches STORE to `copy_bounded` directly, and wraps both `DeflateDecoder` and `zstd::stream::Decoder` in `copy_bounded` for DEFLATE and ZSTD, ensuring all three paths enforce the same output bound.
`decode_payload` returns `LimitExceeded` when `expected_output_size > max_output_size` before constructing any decompressor.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.3: decoded output for all three compression algorithms is bounded by max_output_size via copy_bounded before any output reaches the caller; the limit is enforced using checked arithmetic before each write.

findings.title: BSDIFF and VCDIFF resource limits are correctly derived from unified `ResourceLimits` and enforced before allocation
findings.summary: `bsdiff_limits_from_resource_limits` and `vcdiff_limits_from_resource_limits` in `crates/sar-archive/src/archive.rs` map all relevant ResourceLimits fields to their algorithm-specific structs before patch application. BsdiffLimits covers patch size, control bytes, diff bytes, extra bytes, control triple count, and reconstructed target size. VcdiffLimits covers patch size, window count, instruction count, and output size. Both patch algorithms additionally verify that reconstructed output length equals the declared target size, failing closed on any mismatch. All limit checks in the application paths use early-return error paths before allocating or growing buffers.

evidence.description: `bsdiff_limits_from_resource_limits` and `vcdiff_limits_from_resource_limits` map ResourceLimits fields to BsdiffLimits and VcdiffLimits; `max_in_memory_buffer` bounds the compressed patch size, `max_decoded_entry_size` bounds target output.
`apply_bsdiff` checks `patch_len > limits.max_patch_size` as its first operation before any allocation or parsing; downstream limit checks use early-return error paths before each growth operation.

`VcdiffLimits` documents default bounds for patch size (256 MiB), window count (4 096), instruction count (65 536), and output size (max_decoded_entry_size); all are checked before the corresponding allocation or loop iteration.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.3: BSDIFF and VCDIFF limits are derived from unified ResourceLimits and enforced before allocations and loop iterations in both patch application paths; output length is verified against the declared target size.

findings.title: Sparse reconstruction allocates output bounded by `max_decoded_entry_size` and `max_allocation_bytes` before any allocation
findings.summary: `apply_sparse_reconstruction` checks `logical_size` against both `max_decoded_entry_size` and `max_allocation_bytes` (via `SparseLimits`) before allocating the output Vec. Extent validation uses `checked_add` for offset-plus-length arithmetic with explicit overflow detection. Extents must be non-overlapping, in ascending offset order, and within `logical_size`; zero-length extents, out-of-bounds extents, excess descriptor count, and excess payload bytes are all rejected before the output is returned. `SparseLimits` is derived from `ResourceLimits` via `sparse_limits()` using the tighter of `max_in_memory_buffer` and `max_total_pipeline_memory`.

evidence.description: `apply_sparse_reconstruction` calls `limits.check_decoded_entry_size(logical_size)` and `limits.allocation_len(logical_size)` before `vec![0u8; logical_size_usize]`, bounding output allocation by both limits.

evidence.description: `validate_sparse_extents` checks descriptor count limit, rejects zero-length extents, uses `checked_add` for `offset + length`, rejects out-of-bounds extents, rejects overlapping extents, and rejects excess payload bytes after all extents are consumed.
`sparse_limits()` sets `max_allocation_bytes` as `min(max_in_memory_buffer, max_total_pipeline_memory)` to apply the tighter of the two limits.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.3: sparse reconstruction output is bounded by max_decoded_entry_size and max_allocation_bytes before allocation; extent validation uses checked arithmetic and fails closed for all malformed extent descriptors.

findings.title: Fragment group validation enforces count, span, and loss-tolerant gap limits before reassembly allocation

findings.title: SAR documentation does not state that decompressor internal memory is outside `ResourceLimits`
findings.summary: `DecompressionOptions.max_output_size` is documented as a decoded-output cap, and SAR constructs both Deflate and Zstd decoders without a SAR-specific decoder-memory budget parameter. The public `ResourceLimits` surface does not expose a field dedicated to decoder library-internal state. Current SAR documentation therefore does not clearly state that decoded output is bounded by SAR limits while decoder-library working memory remains outside any explicitly documented SAR `ResourceLimits` field.
findings.impact: Operators and integrators reading the SAR limit surface can tell how decoded output is bounded, but they cannot tell from SAR documentation whether decoder-library internal state is separately bounded, unbounded, or intentionally delegated to dependency defaults. The evidence supports a documentation deficiency, not a demonstrated safety defect.

evidence.description: `DecompressionOptions` documents only `max_output_size` as a hard cap for decoded bytes to prevent decompression bombs; it does not describe any bound on decoder-library internal memory.
The DEFLATE path constructs `DeflateDecoder::new(input)` and the ZSTD path constructs `zstd::stream::Decoder::new(input)` without passing a SAR-defined decoder-memory limit parameter.

`ResourceLimits` documents decoded-entry, per-buffer, and total-pipeline bounds, but it does not define a decoder-library-memory-specific field or document such memory as covered by an existing field.

requirements: Document in the public compression and resource-limit API documentation that `max_output_size` bounds decoded output bytes only.
Document that DEFLATE/ZSTD decoder library-internal working memory is not currently represented by a dedicated SAR `ResourceLimits` field.
If a future SAR-specific decoder-memory control is added, document which field governs it and how it interacts with decoded-output limits.

findings.title: FEC value byte length and parity allocation are bounded before codec construction

Stripe count, group count, and parity length products use `checked_mul` and `checked_add` throughout both codecs. findings.title: In-memory recovery API documents limitations and applies archive-size, protected-range, and partial working-set bounds

evidence.locator: module documentation for archive recovery APIs
evidence.description: Module documentation explicitly states in-memory API limitations and instructs callers to enforce `max_archive_size`, `max_recovery_protected_range`, and `max_repair_working_set` before passing untrusted archives.

findings.title: `TransportConfig` propagates only `max_active_streams` to the `ResourceLimits` used by `StreamArchiveParser` and `SessionManager`
findings.summary: `TransportStreamContext::new()` constructs the transport-layer `ResourceLimits` by copying only `max_active_streams` from `TransportConfig` and applying `ResourceLimits::default()` for every other field. The public transport API does not document this fixed-default boundary contract, so callers may misread `TransportConfig` as a broader resource-limit surface than the transport actually honors.
findings.current_behavior: The transport layer always constructs `ResourceLimits { max_active_streams: config.max_active_sar_streams, ..ResourceLimits::default() }`. `TransportConfig` documents its own fields but does not explain that the remaining parser and session `ResourceLimits` stay fixed at transport defaults.
findings.expected_behavior: The `TransportConfig` and `InMemoryTransport` documentation should state that the transport layer fixes all inner `ResourceLimits` fields at their defaults except `max_active_streams`, so callers understand the effective transport-layer limit contract.
findings.impact: Callers may assume that configuring `TransportConfig` also changes parser or session limits that in fact remain fixed at defaults, leading to incorrect expectations about the transport-layer resource contract.

evidence.description: Only `max_active_streams` is taken from `config.max_active_sar_streams`; all other `ResourceLimits` fields use defaults, which is not documented in `TransportConfig` or `InMemoryTransport`.
The field documents only its own limit, without stating that corresponding `ResourceLimits` fields for per-entry memory, output size, or session limits are unaffected by `TransportConfig`.

requirements: Document in `TransportConfig` and `InMemoryTransport` that the transport layer fixes all inner `ResourceLimits` fields at their defaults except `max_active_streams`.
State the effective transport-layer limit contract without implying that `TransportConfig` currently provides broader parser, fragment, or session-limit configurability.

findings.title: `validate_archive_profile` is documented as global-header-only and does not provide entry-level algorithm, loss-tolerant, or path-safety enforcement
findings.summary: `validate_archive_profile` checks only global-header flags and explicitly documents that entry-level algorithm ID checks, per-entry `LOSS_TOLERANT` enforcement, and unsafe filesystem metadata rejection are not implemented. The reviewed public `sar-archive` profile surface contains `ComplianceProfile`, `ProfileReport`, `validate_archive_profile`, and profile name conversion helpers; no reviewed public entry-iterating profile-validation entry point was identified. The `Standard` profile variant returns a placeholder finding rather than enforcing conformance. Callers relying on `validate_archive_profile` alone have incomplete profile assurance for the entry-level requirements of `StaticArchive`, `Package`, `Backup`, and `Standard` profiles. The profile API surface does not guide callers toward completing those checks. This finding is distinct from M13-TRANSFORM-001, which addresses the missing normative algorithm table; the current finding addresses the absence of a reviewed public entry-level enforcement entry point.
findings.current_behavior: `validate_archive_profile` documents in its docstring that entry-level LOSS_TOLERANT presence, algorithm ID restrictions, and unsafe path rejection are unimplemented. The `Standard` variant pushes a placeholder finding instead of validating conformance.
findings.expected_behavior: Document a complete public workflow for entry-level profile validation, or provide a public entry-iterating validation entry point that reports the remaining profile checks.
findings.impact: A library caller who calls `validate_archive_profile` and observes `compliant: true` may incorrectly conclude that all profile requirements are satisfied for `StaticArchive`, `Package`, `Backup`, or `Telemetry`. Missing entry-level enforcement is not surfaced as a limitation at the call site.

evidence.description: The function documents that entry-level LOSS_TOLERANT checks, algorithm ID checks, and unsafe filesystem metadata rejection are not implemented and that Standard profile validation is a placeholder.

The public profile inventory enumerates `ComplianceProfile::canonical_name`, `ComplianceProfile::from_canonical_name`, `validate_archive_profile`, `ComplianceProfile`, and `ProfileReport`; no public entry-iterating profile-validation API is listed.

notes: The missing normative algorithm restriction tables are tracked separately in M13-TRANSFORM-001. This finding concerns the API boundary: no entry-level profile enforcement entry point exists in the public library API.

requirements: Document at the `validate_archive_profile` call site which profile requirements are not covered and which entry-iteration or extraction-layer checks are needed to complete profile enforcement.
Document a complete public workflow for entry-level profile validation, or provide a public entry-iterating validation entry point that reports the remaining profile checks.

findings.title: Transport inactivity watchdog is caller-driven and the opt-in requirement is not documented in `TransportConfig` or `InMemoryTransport`
findings.summary: `TransportConfig` exposes `heartbeat_min_interval_ms`, `heartbeat_required_interval_ms`, and `inactivity_timeout_ms`, but watchdog evaluation is performed only when callers explicitly supply `now_ms` to `TcpSarConnection::process_available` or call `InMemoryTransport::check_inactivity` directly. Passing `now_ms = None` skips all time-based checks silently. The opt-in requirement is documented in `TcpSarConnection::process_available` but not in `TransportConfig`, `InMemoryTransport`, or the QUIC connection APIs. Callers reading only the configuration struct may believe the timeout is enforced automatically.
findings.current_behavior: Watchdog evaluation requires explicit `now_ms = Some(...)` input in every `process_available` call, or explicit `check_inactivity` invocation. No background thread or timer is used. Calls with `now_ms = None` skip all time-based checks.
findings.expected_behavior: `TransportConfig` documentation should state that timeout fields are effective only when callers supply explicit timestamps, and that no background enforcement occurs. `InMemoryTransport` documentation should describe the required caller-side watchdog polling pattern.
findings.impact: Callers who configure `inactivity_timeout_ms` but pass `now_ms = None` get no timeout enforcement. The misconfiguration is silent.

evidence.description: The docstring states that `now_ms` controls heartbeat and watchdog checks and that `None` skips time-based checks, but this opt-in is not restated at the `TransportConfig` or `InMemoryTransport` level.
These fields document their value semantics but do not state the caller-side activation requirement.
The test drives `check_inactivity` with explicit timestamps and verifies that the configured inactivity timeout is evaluated from those supplied values.

requirements: Add documentation to `TransportConfig` stating that timeout and heartbeat fields are effective only when callers supply explicit timestamps.
Document the expected polling pattern for `check_inactivity` in `InMemoryTransport` and `QuicSarConnection` where applicable.

findings.title: `QuicSarConnection::feed_stream_bytes` accumulates outbound control frames but the required follow-up `flush_pending_control_frames` call is not documented in the public method
findings.summary: `QuicSarConnection::feed_stream_bytes` processes inbound bytes and serialises outbound `SESSION_ACK` and `SESSION_STATUS` frames into an internal `pending_control_bytes` buffer. These bytes are NOT written to the wire by `feed_stream_bytes`. Callers must call `flush_pending_control_frames` after each `feed_stream_bytes` call to emit queued control frames. The required ordering is documented only in the private `pending_control_bytes` field comment; it is absent from the public `feed_stream_bytes` docstring. Callers who do not read the source may silently drop outbound control frames on the affected QUIC stream.
findings.current_behavior: `feed_stream_bytes` accumulates outbound frames in `pending_control_bytes` but does not flush them. The flush obligation is documented in the private field comment only.
findings.expected_behavior: The `feed_stream_bytes` docstring should state that callers must call `flush_pending_control_frames` after each invocation when bidirectional control is enabled.
findings.impact: Callers who omit the `flush_pending_control_frames` step silently drop outbound `SESSION_ACK` and `SESSION_STATUS` frames, breaking bidirectional session control without any error return.

evidence.description: The private field comment states: 'Callers must flush these via `flush_pending_control_frames` after each call to `feed_stream_bytes`.' This requirement is not surfaced in the public method docstring.
The public docstring does not mention the flush requirement or reference `flush_pending_control_frames`.
Async method that drains `pending_control_bytes` to the QUIC stream send side. Must be called after `feed_stream_bytes` to emit outbound control frames.

requirements: Add a `flush_pending_control_frames` call requirement to the `feed_stream_bytes` docstring, specifying that callers must flush after each invocation when bidirectional control is active.

findings.title: `InMemoryTransport` enforces TLS_EXPORTER fail-closed behavior at the transport parsing layer for primary and attached control streams
findings.summary: After `SESSION_INIT` processing succeeds with `KMS_TLS_EXPORTER` mode, `InMemoryTransport` inserts the SAR Stream ID into `tls_exporter_bound`. All subsequent entries on the primary stream and on attached QUIC control streams are rejected with `SarError::AuthFailed` if `EntryMode::ENCRYPTED` is not set. The transport never falls back to plaintext after binding. This extends the AEAD-level fail-closed control recorded in M13-CRYPTO-004 to the transport session boundary, providing a defense-in-depth check that does not depend on downstream AEAD decryption succeeding.

evidence.locator: struct `InMemoryTransport`, field `tls_exporter_bound` and `SESSION_INIT` handling block that calls `tls_exporter_bound.insert()`
evidence.description: The `tls_exporter_bound` set is populated on successful `SESSION_INIT` with `KMS_TLS_EXPORTER`, and the transport subsequently rejects unencrypted entries with `SarError::AuthFailed` before any downstream processing.
The first test verifies primary-stream plaintext rejection after TLS_EXPORTER binding, and the second verifies additional-control-stream plaintext rejection after TLS_EXPORTER binding.

notes: This is a transport-layer defense-in-depth control. The AEAD-level fail-closed behavior is recorded separately in M13-CRYPTO-004.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.5: `InMemoryTransport` populates `tls_exporter_bound` after `SESSION_INIT` and rejects unencrypted entries at the transport layer with `SarError::AuthFailed`.

findings.title: `KeyProvider` trait callback model requires a purpose-built stable wrapper for any foreign-language binding
findings.summary: The `KeyProvider` trait is a required parameter for encryption-capable archive reading (`ArchiveReader::with_key_provider`, `StreamArchiveParser::with_key_provider`) and for transport-layer key provisioning in `InMemoryTransport::with_key_provider`. The trait requires `Send + Sync` and uses Rust-specific callback semantics: methods return `Result<Option<SecretBytes | SecretString>, SarCryptoError>`. A foreign-language binding cannot implement this trait directly because it requires a stable callback ABI, foreign-side memory ownership of `SecretBytes`/`SecretString` across the call boundary, and mapping of `SarCryptoError` to a stable error type. A purpose-built stable wrapper API is required that accepts foreign function pointers and manages key-material ownership and destruction without exposing zeroizing containers to foreign callers. The API inventory acknowledges this requirement in the `KeyProvider` FFI notes.
findings.current_behavior: Encryption-capable archive and transport APIs require a `Box<dyn KeyProvider>` or `Arc<dyn KeyProvider>`. No stable callback-to-trait adapter is provided.
findings.expected_behavior: Library documentation should identify `KeyProvider` as the primary FFI boundary blocker for encryption-capable APIs and describe the required wrapper design: foreign function pointer model, key-material ownership, and destruction semantics.
findings.impact: A naive C or Python binding to `ArchiveReader::with_key_provider` or `InMemoryTransport::with_key_provider` is not possible without an intermediate Rust-side adapter layer. The absence of documentation leaves wrapper authors to discover this limitation independently.

evidence.locator: trait `KeyProvider`, trait bounds `Send + Sync`, method return types `Result<Option<SecretBytes>, SarCryptoError>` and `Result<Option<SecretString>, SarCryptoError>`
evidence.description: The trait requires `Send + Sync` and returns Rust-specific owned secret containers. No extern-fn or callback-pointer interface is provided.
API inventory marks `KeyProvider` as `readiness: unstable` with note that a dedicated callback design is required for Milestone 12.

notes: `SecretBytes` and `SecretString` are Rust-specific zeroizing containers marked `candidate: false` in the API inventory. Key material returned via a foreign callback must be owned and destroyed by the Rust wrapper without crossing the FFI boundary as a raw pointer to these types.

requirements: Document `KeyProvider` as the primary FFI blocker for encryption-capable archive and transport APIs.
Describe the required wrapper design: foreign function pointer callback, key-material ownership transfer model, and destruction/zeroization responsibility.

findings.title: `SarError::Io(std::io::Error)` holds a Rust-specific owned type that cannot be directly exposed across a C or Python boundary
findings.summary: `SarError` is the primary error type returned by all public SAR library APIs. Its `Io` variant holds a `std::io::Error`, which is a Rust-specific owned type that is not ABI-stable and whose internal representation may vary by Rust version and platform. A stable C or Python wrapper must map `SarError` to an integer status code (the `SarStatus` numeric code system is already designed for this purpose) and optionally a caller-owned message buffer, discarding the `std::io::Error` before crossing the language boundary. The API inventory notes for `SarError` document this as a preference but do not specify the mapping requirement. No stable wrapper exists.
findings.current_behavior: `SarError` variants include `Io(std::io::Error)`, `NotFound(&'static str)`, and others, none of which are ABI-stable or safely exposable to foreign callers.
findings.expected_behavior: Library documentation and wrapper design guidance should specify the canonical `SarStatus`-based numeric mapping for `SarError`, the expected message-buffer ownership model, and that `std::io::Error` is discarded or reduced to a string before crossing the FFI boundary.
findings.impact: Wrapper authors must independently discover the `SarStatus` mapping and message-ownership conventions. The mapping is not currently documented at the `SarError` or `SarStatus` level.

evidence.description: `SarError` includes a `std::io::Error` variant and string-slice variants. Neither is ABI-stable or safely passable to foreign callers.
API inventory notes: 'Prefer mapping to a stable status enum plus opaque message buffers for FFI.' The specific mapping to `SarStatus` codes is not documented.

requirements: Document the canonical `SarStatus`-based numeric mapping from `SarError` variants for use in stable wrapper APIs.
Specify how `std::io::Error` should be reduced or discarded before the status code is returned to foreign callers.
Describe message-buffer ownership semantics for the optional string portion of the error.

findings.title: Public QUIC connection and stream I/O operations are async and require a runtime adapter for synchronous foreign wrappers
findings.summary: The listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs (`connect_quic`, `QuicSarListener::accept`, `QuicSarConnection::open_sar_stream`, `QuicSarConnection::accept_sar_stream`, `QuicSarConnection::write_sar_bytes`, `QuicSarConnection::read_stream_bytes`, `QuicSarConnection::flush_pending_control_frames`) are `async fn` and return `Future` values that require a Tokio executor. These operations cannot be directly exposed through synchronous C or Python wrappers without a blocking adapter or event-loop integration layer. Other QUIC-facing public APIs such as `bind`, `local_addr`, `close`, `feed_stream_bytes`, `local_capabilities`, and TLS-exporter helpers are synchronous, so the gap is limited to the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs. The synchronous TCP binding (`TcpSarConnection`) remains more amenable to blocking foreign wrappers. The runtime requirement is not documented at the affected QUIC APIs.
findings.current_behavior: The listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs are async. No blocking wrapper or Tokio handle is provided. The TCP binding is synchronous and blocking.
findings.expected_behavior: The documentation for the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs should note the Tokio runtime requirement and state that direct C or Python binding requires a blocking adapter layer or runtime handle. The TCP binding should be identified as the more FFI-amenable synchronous transport option.
findings.impact: A naive foreign binding to the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs, such as `QuicSarListener::accept` or `connect_quic`, will not compile or execute correctly without a Tokio runtime. The runtime requirement is not surfaced in the public API documentation.

evidence.description: All listed public methods are declared `pub async fn`. Docstrings do not state the Tokio runtime dependency, while other QUIC-facing public APIs in the same module remain synchronous.
Synchronous blocking TCP methods. No async executor is required.

requirements: Document the Tokio runtime requirement on the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs.
Note that `TcpSarConnection` is the synchronous transport option for blocking FFI wrappers.
Describe the blocking adapter or runtime handle pattern required for synchronous C or Python QUIC integration.
